action_criteria.expected_evidence: AChR binding antibody 0.6 nmol/L above the 0.5 cut-off with raised blocking and modulating antibodies; TSH and free T4 normal.
action_criteria.label: Order AChR binding antibody and thyroid function
action_criteria.rationale: Fatigable ptosis, diplopia, dysphagia for liquids and neck flexor weakness point to generalized MG; AChR binding antibody is the first test (Jacob 2025, Evoli 2019), and thyroid function is tested in every MG patient, all the more with her polyautoimmunity.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Borderline 8-10% decrement at 3 Hz with post-exercise exhaustion, normal baseline CMAP and no facilitation.
action_criteria.label: Order repetitive nerve stimulation including facial and proximal muscles
action_criteria.rationale: Neurophysiology confirms the junctional disorder and excludes a presynaptic pattern (Jacob 2025).

action_criteria.rationale: No muscle exceeds the 10% decrement threshold, so SFEMG gives the neurophysiological confirmation; positive serology makes it recommended rather than required.

action_criteria.rationale: Mediastinal imaging is indicated in every patient with MG; a thymoma would change the surgical plan, and its absence makes her an MGTX-type thymectomy candidate.

action_criteria.rationale: Dysphagia with nasal regurgitation and marked neck flexor weakness: baseline respiratory muscle strength stages the disease and sets escalation thresholds (Lawn 2001).

prohibited_recommendations: Avoid fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides, macrolides and IV magnesium unless no alternative exists and the patient is monitored; use non-depolarising neuromuscular blockers only at reduced dose with quantitative monitoring.

Do not start high-dose prednisone (above 20 mg/day) as an outpatient; start low and titrate, or start high dose only with inpatient monitoring, because initial steroid-induced worsening can precipitate crisis.
Do not attribute fatigable ptosis, diplopia or bulbar weakness to a functional or lupus-related cause before AChR antibody testing and neurophysiology.
Do not increase hydroxychloroquine further; it can impair neuromuscular transmission.
required_recommendations: Start pyridostigmine 30 mg orally three to four times daily and titrate to effect (usually 60 mg four to five times daily), watching for muscarinic effects that pilocarpine adds to.

Start prednisone either low (10-20 mg/day, increased by 5-10 mg every 3-7 days) or at high dose only with inpatient monitoring, because steroid initiation can transiently worsen MG; give a proton pump inhibitor while she takes prednisone with celecoxib.
Choose a steroid-sparing agent with rheumatology (azathioprine after TPMT/NUDT15 testing, or mycophenolate with contraception counseling), since both treat SLE as well as MG.
Offer elective thymectomy once MG is controlled: AChR-positive generalized MG without thymoma at age 48 (MGTX, Wolfe 2016).

Ask rheumatology to bring hydroxychloroquine back to no more than 5 mg/kg/day (for example 200 mg daily at 58.5 kg) and not to increase it, because it can worsen MG and the current 400 mg exceeds the retinal-safety dose.

Repeat FVC, MIP and MEP at least daily while bulbar and neck weakness persist, with ICU-level care if FVC falls below 20 mL/kg, MIP is weaker than -30 cmH2O, MEP falls below 40 cmH2O or cough and secretions worsen; swallow assessment before thin liquids.

avoided_actions.rationale: MG is a disorder of the neuromuscular junction; EEG has no diagnostic role here (Jacob 2025).
CSF has no role in MG; she has no ataxia, areflexia or CNS sign to raise a CSF-informative alternative (Jacob 2025).
FDG-PET is not indicated in MG; mediastinal CT answers the thymoma question (Jacob 2025).
Brain MRI is reserved for negative serology and neurophysiology or a central mimic; she has positive AChR antibodies and no central signs (Jacob 2025).
No cardiac question in this patient; echocardiography does not contribute to MG diagnosis or staging.
No arrhythmia or autonomic symptom in this patient; cardiac monitoring does not contribute to MG diagnosis or staging.

accepted: Myasthenia gravis, generalized (MGFA Class IIb), AChR antibody-positive, without thymoma, in setting of SLE/Sjögren overlap (polyautoimmunity)

differential.key_features: SLE myopathy causes proximal weakness without fatigable ptosis or diplopia; CK is normal (118 U/L), needle EMG shows no fibrillation potentials, and the decrement and jitter point to the neuromuscular junction.
Sjogren neuropathy is sensory-predominant; sensation and nerve conduction studies are normal and it does not cause fatigable ptosis or diplopia.

LEMS gives low baseline CMAPs with post-exercise facilitation, areflexia and autonomic symptoms; here CMAPs are normal, post-exercise increment is 4%, reflexes are normal and AChR antibodies are positive.
Hydroxychloroquine can unmask or worsen MG, but symptoms began before the dose increase and positive AChR antibodies indicate autoimmune MG; HCQ is at most an aggravating factor.
No long-tract or sensory signs; weakness is fatigable and involves several cranial and limb muscle groups, a pattern a focal brainstem lesion does not explain.

key_clinical_evidence: Fatigable asymmetric ptosis, diplopia, dysphagia for liquids with nasal regurgitation, neck flexor and proximal arm weakness worse at the end of the day: generalized MG with bulbar involvement (MGFA IIb).
AChR binding antibody 0.6 nmol/L is above the laboratory cut-off of 0.5 and therefore positive, supported by raised blocking and modulating antibodies.
RNS is equivocal (maximum 10% decrement) and SFEMG shows increased jitter with blocking.
Mediastinal CT with contrast is indicated in every patient with MG to detect thymoma. Here it shows a fatty involuted thymus without thymoma.
MIP -38 cmH2O and MEP 58 cmH2O with neck flexor weakness: respiratory muscle involvement to follow serially.
Polyautoimmunity (SLE, Sjogren syndrome, MG) is well described; mild serological lupus activity does not explain fatigable bulbar and ocular weakness.
Hydroxychloroquine, pilocarpine and celecoxib each matter for MG treatment: possible aggravation, added muscarinic effects, and gastrointestinal risk with prednisone.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Mild SLE activity does not explain fatigable ptosis, diplopia, dysphagia, or RNS decrement; AChR antibodies are diagnostic; SLE comorbidity is real but separate.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute fatigable weakness to lupus flare or lupus myositis and pursue SLE treatment escalation instead of MG workup.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A value above the laboratory cut-off is positive; with raised blocking and modulating antibodies and a typical clinical picture it supports AChR-positive MG.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Dismiss as a non-specific positive in the setting of polyautoimmunity.

sequence_constraints.reason: AChR antibody testing precedes single-fiber EMG; SFEMG is reserved for seronegative patients or a normal RNS (Jacob 2025).
Repetitive nerve stimulation is done first; SFEMG follows when RNS is normal (Jacob 2025).

contraindications: Pyridostigmine: mechanical intestinal or urinary obstruction.

Celecoxib: product labeling lists sulfonamide allergy as a contraindication. Sulfa allergy (rash) is recorded; cross-reactivity between sulfonamide antibiotics and non-antibiotic sulfonamides is uncommon and the drug is currently tolerated. Review with the prescriber.
pyridostigmine.formulary_status: Pyridostigmine bromide 60 mg tablets: formulary; prednisone: formulary
interactions: Pyridostigmine + pilocarpine: additive muscarinic effects (sweating, hypersalivation, diarrhea, abdominal cramps, bradycardia, bronchial secretions). Monitor; use the lowest effective doses and review the pilocarpine dose if muscarinic symptoms appear.
Hydroxychloroquine: case reports of new or worsened myasthenic weakness (impaired neuromuscular transmission). Avoid dose increases; monitor weakness; review the dose with the prescriber.
Prednisone + celecoxib: corticosteroid with an NSAID increases the risk of gastrointestinal ulceration and bleeding. Consider gastroprotection with a proton pump inhibitor.
Pyridostigmine + celecoxib: no clinically relevant interaction.
pyridostigmine.summary: Two interactions to manage (pilocarpine with pyridostigmine; celecoxib with prednisone) and one drug that can worsen MG (hydroxychloroquine).
warnings: Hydroxychloroquine: retinal toxicity risk rises with doses above 5 mg/kg actual body weight per day.
Drugs that impair neuromuscular transmission (aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, macrolides, IV magnesium, neuromuscular blockers, beta-blockers) can worsen myasthenic weakness.

labs.interpretation: Anti-AChR binding antibody positive at low titre (0.6 nmol/L, reference <0.5), with raised blocking (22%) and modulating (28%) antibodies. Anti-MuSK negative. Anti-dsDNA raised, C3 and C4 low, anti-Ro/SSA positive. Mild anemia (Hb 11.6 g/dL). TSH, free T4, CK, sodium, creatinine and urinalysis within reference ranges. Anti-AChR antibodies are found in most patients with generalized myasthenia gravis; clinical correlation recommended.

results.finding: Pyridostigmine is the initial symptomatic treatment; corticosteroids or immunosuppressive therapy are used when treatment goals are not met; thymectomy is recommended for thymoma and should be considered in AChR-positive generalized MG; IVIG and plasma exchange are used for impending or manifest crisis and before surgery in patients with significant bulbar or respiratory weakness.
results.source: Sanders DB et al., Neurology 2016;87:419-425 (international consensus guidance)

results.finding: Thymectomy recommendations were updated after MGTX for non-thymomatous AChR-positive generalized MG aged 18-65; eculizumab is an option in severe refractory AChR-positive generalized MG; methotrexate may be considered as a steroid-sparing agent.
results.source: Narayanaswami P et al., Neurology 2021;96:114-122 (2020 update)

results.finding: Extended transsternal thymectomy plus prednisone improved the time-weighted quantitative MG score and reduced prednisone requirement over three years compared with prednisone alone in non-thymomatous AChR-positive generalized MG.
results.source: Wolfe GI et al., N Engl J Med 2016;375:511-522 (MGTX)

myasthenia gravis diagnosis thymoma thym.summary: Consensus guidance (Sanders DB et al., Neurology 2016;87:419-425; update Narayanaswami P et al., Neurology 2021;96:114-122) recommends AChR antibody testing first, MuSK testing when AChR antibodies are absent, and electrodiagnostic confirmation by repetitive nerve stimulation or single-fibre EMG. Chest CT or MRI is recommended in all patients to detect thymoma. In the MGTX trial (Wolfe GI et al., N Engl J Med 2016;375:511-522) thymectomy improved outcomes over three years in non-thymomatous AChR-positive generalized MG aged 18-65.

patient.chief_complaint: Fluctuating ptosis, diplopia, and difficulty swallowing liquids

past_medical_history: Systemic lupus erythematosus (stable, skin and joint involvement only)

patient.history_present_illness: A 48-year-old woman with known SLE and Sjögren syndrome was referred to neurology after her rheumatologist noticed bilateral ptosis during a routine follow-up visit. She reports that she first noticed drooping of her right eyelid approximately 5 months ago, which she attributed to fatigue related to her lupus. She initially thought her Sjögren syndrome dry eyes were causing the eyelid heaviness. The ptosis became bilateral over 3 months and was accompanied by intermittent double vision, worse at the end of the day and on sustained lateral gaze. She mentions she has been having trouble swallowing liquids — she occasionally coughs when drinking water rapidly but can swallow solid foods without major difficulty. Her neck feels weak and she has been supporting her chin with her hand during prolonged reading. She initially discussed these symptoms with her rheumatologist, who increased her hydroxychloroquine dose thinking it was a lupus flare — this did not improve the neurological symptoms. She denies headache, sensory loss, or limb weakness at rest, though she notices she tires easily when blow-drying her hair (arm fatigue with overhead activities). She has not had any infections recently. She has a maternal aunt with myasthenia gravis, which her rheumatologist recalled and prompted the neurology referral. Her lupus has been otherwise stable — no joint flares, no rash worsening, no renal involvement. She is on hydroxychloroquine long-term and has had normal ophthalmology retinal checks.

neurological_exam.additional: No respiratory distress at rest. Neck weakness notable; she cannot lift her head off the pillow against resistance.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Bilateral ptosis, right greater than left. Fatigable ptosis on sustained upgaze — ptosis becomes complete on right side at 55 seconds. Diplopia on upgaze and rightward gaze. Mild left eye adduction weakness. Pupils equal and reactive. Mild dysarthria after sustained speech (>2 minutes). No facial sensory deficit. Palate symmetric at rest but slight nasal regurgitation of water on examination.
neurological_exam.gait: Normal casual gait. Mild waddling pattern on prolonged walking.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented x4. Normal language and cognition.
neurological_exam.motor: Proximal upper extremity: deltoids 4/5 bilaterally. Neck flexors: 3+/5. Distal strength preserved. Demonstrable fatigability — neck flexion strength drops from 3+ to 3-/5 after 30 seconds sustained effort.

physical_exam.general: Weight 58.5 kg, height 162 cm. Well appearing.
physical_exam.respiratory: Chest clear. No accessory muscle use. Cough slightly weak.
physical_exam.skin: No malar rash. No active synovitis.
